title: using dynamic memory to avoid reference invalidation
body_html:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <cstring>

using namespace std; //please ignore bad practices like this and everything being set to public. Its just for sake of demonstration.

vector<int>& f() {
    vector<int> a = *new vector<int>{15, 15, 16};
    return a;
}

int main () {
    vector<int>& b = f();
    
    for (auto x: b) {
        cout << x << endl;
    }
delete &b;
    
    cout << "finished" << endl;
}

Hi:

In the code above, I'm using dynamic allocated memory so that vector a would have its memory stored on the heap, so it can avoid getting deleted after the function exits. But for some reason it didn't. The code gives me this error that can't be understood:

events.body_html: vector<int> a = *new vector<int>{15, 15, 16}; doesn't work the way you think it would. You seem to assume that a "has its memory stored on the heap" because an unrelated vector at the right hand side of the initialisation has. Do you have Java or C# background by any chance?

vector<int>& f() {
    vector<int> a = *new vector<int>{15, 15, 16};
    return a;
}

This is calling the copy constructor of a and passing the heap allocated object to it. a is not created on the heap. It is destroyed when f() exits, leaving the returned reference dangling, and the heap allocated vector leaked after the constructor.

Use a reference instead of a second object. Just bind the already created vector on the heap to the reference that gets returned.

vector<int>& f() {
    vector<int>& a = *new vector<int>{15, 15, 16};
    return a;
}

While this may work, This is bad design

A reference is a non-owning construct, it doesn't manage the object's lifetime, while your code expects the caller to delete the object, this is a memory leak waiting to happen.

The proper way to make this code work is to simply return the vector from your function and let the compiler move it:

vector<int> f() {
    vector<int> a{15, 15, 16};
    return a;
}
...
vector<int> b = f();
@n.m.couldbeanAI  Java background only. The whole memory management deal is a bit new to me.
Every time you see X a = *new X you see two things (1) a confused Java refugee and (2) a memory leak. Java knowledge does not transfer to C++.

In interests of completeness, you might wish to clarify (1) The OP's code doesn't only return a dangling reference (due to destruction of a) - it also leaks the vector created by the new expression. (2) As you say, your first code sample works but is bad design - and that is because it forces the caller to explicitly release the newed vector (via an unnecessarily clumsy syntax to obtain a pointer from the reference, and deleteing it) or, if the caller omits that, the result is another member leak.
Yep, I'm aware that you need to delete stuff using "delete" keyword to pointer towards the original object itself on the stack. But yeah I omitted it here bc its just for the sake of example.

@NathanPierson I edited my code to add delete --- can you check if its done correctly? In addition, is there a way to check it myself?

Actually, your understanding of how new and delete pair together isn't quite right. Your delete applies to a different vector than the one you originally new'd. When you wrote new vector<int>{15, 15, 16}, the vector that was created here was copied to initialize a, but a pointer to it was never stored anywhere in the program. Then a was destroyed at the end of f() because it had automatic storage duration, but because b is a dangling reference to it you try to delete it again. But you never tried to delete the original vector, and in fact cannot.
"I edited my code to add delete" That's not the pointer you have received from the new operator. That pointer is irretrievably lost at the moment X a = *new X; sees its semicolon.
And in any case std::vector is not something you normally new. std::vector is sort of a smart pointer by itself. It manages its own memory.
